comment: The redaction rule set: the names and the patterns the redactor uses,
written out once so an implementation can be checked against them.
The implementation is the Rust crate
crates/sasy-redaction, used in one place: the LLM oracle
path in sasy-policy, which scrubs a query before it leaves the host.
That crate has a test reading this file and comparing it to its own
constants, so a name added to the crate and not to this file fails its
suite. Nothing scrubs at ingest.
The rules are written to stay portable across regular-expression
engines: the notes below record why a pattern is written the way it
is, including where an engine without backtracking or lookahead needs
a different spelling of the same rule. This file is not loaded at run
time; an implementation keeps its own copy of the names and shapes.
Every name here is compared ASCII-case-insensitively. A Unicode fold
would make `--paſsword=`, `?Key=` and `cooKie` match a
name, so the folding is ASCII-only in every pattern that carries a
name. One comparison is not a pattern: the structural URL pass
lowercases a query-parameter name in code before looking it up, and
that fold is ASCII-only too (`to_ascii_lowercase`), so
`https://h/v1?Key=` carries a name the rules do not know.
params_comment: Parameter names come in two tiers. A name in `query_params_unambiguous`
means a credential wherever it stands, so it is redacted after any
`param_delimiter` - `--password=x` on a command line as much as
`?password=x` in a URL. A name in `query_params_query_string_only` is an
ordinary word elsewhere, so it is only redacted after a
`query_string_delimiter`: `?key=x` and `&key=x` are credentials,
`session=requests.Session()` and a `key=value` line in a config file are
content and are left byte-identical. The structural URL pass - a run with
a scheme, or a `host/path?...` form - is inside a query string already, so
it treats both tiers alike and splits fields on `query_separator`. It
counts one name more than the two tiers list: a field whose last
hyphen-separated segment is `signature` or `sig`, which is the
credential that makes a pre-signed URL work - `X-Amz-Signature`,
`X-Goog-Signature`. The segment has to be the whole of it, so `?design=`
and `?resig=` are content.
`param_value` excludes the backslash so a value in JSON-encoded text stops
before the escape of the closing quote, leaving the blob parseable and the
rest of the field - a recorded command's destination URL - intact.
One dotted form is read on top of `param_delimiter`, which excludes the
`.` and so left every dotted spelling unread: an unambiguous name with a
`.` in front of it and the `=` GLUED to it, no space and no quote between
them - `spring.datasource.password=`, `db.password=`,
`mail.smtp.password=`, `-Dspring.datasource.password=` and
`--set postgres.password=`. The value is read by the same literal
grammar. Nothing else about the dotted name is read: the spaced
assignment (`self.password = get_pw()`, `config.api_key =
settings.API_KEY`) and the colon form
(`spring.datasource.password: hunter2hunter2`) stay unread, because the
exclusion of the `.` is what keeps ordinary source from being rewritten.
Both are stated limits.
`param_delimiter` counts the two-character escapes `\n`, `\r` and
`\t` as a delimiter alongside the real characters. A file body reaches
this code JSON encoded - a Write's `content`, an Edit's replacement, a
Read result, a tool argument - and there a line break is the two
characters `\` and `n`, not one newline. Reading the backslash as the
delimiter left `n` to begin the name, so every name on the second or
later line of a written or read `.env` file went unread and the
credential was stored whole.
header_comment: A credential header is read three ways here and a fourth in a serialised
map. The map reading - a quoted `"name": value` pair, value a string or
a one-element array - is unchanged. The other reading finds the name
after a `header_boundary` (the start, one of the two-character escapes
`\n`, `\r` and `\t`, a quote, whitespace, `=`, `(`, `,`
or one of `[`, `{`, `|`), which covers a line of its own, a raw header
block inside a JSON-encoded file body or tool result, a
`curl -H "..."`, a JavaScript object literal, a bracketed log line, a
markdown table cell, a `> ` trace
line and a log line with a timestamp in front of it. Between the name
and its colon stands the `header_name_separator`, the same optional
backslash-and-quote the `name_value_separator` carries, so a header
name is read where a JSON blob has been encoded into a string a second
time and the name arrives as `\"authorization\"`. Without it the seven
header-only names - authorization, proxy-authorization, cookie,
set-cookie, x-auth-token, x-goog-api-key, x-subscription-token - were
unreachable in double-encoded text and the credential was stored whole.
What follows the
colon is read three ways. When a quote opens the value - `authorization:
"Basic ..."`, which is how every YAML config, JavaScript object literal
and TOML file writes a header whose NAME is not quoted - the value is a
quoted literal read by the literal grammar, quotes kept and content
gone. Otherwise, with a space after the colon the value runs to
the end of the line or to a `header_value_terminators` character, and
what counts as the credential depends on the header: a `scheme_headers`
value is `<scheme> <token>` or a bare token - the scheme word is ASCII
letters - and nothing else. A value carrying a token past
that shape is a sentence (`There are three kinds of authorization: role,
attribute and policy.`, `def check(authorization: str, cookie: str) ->
bool:`) unless the candidate is made only of `literal_value_chars` and
is a credential by the literal grammar, which is what keeps a log line's
`authorization: Bearer eyJ... host: api.example.com` reading while the
`host:` field survives. Inside the two-token shape - and only there -
the value is a credential whatever it looks like: `Basic dXNlcjpwYXNz`
is base64 that may hold no digit. A `cookie_headers` value is
the rest of the line and must contain an `=`, and every other header
takes a single token, which is a credential only when it is made of
`literal_value_chars`, passes the literal grammar and is not a WORD.
A word is a value made solely of letters, digits, `-`, `/`, `.` and `_`
with no digit anywhere in it: `application/json`, `not-set`,
`role-based`, `user-provided`, `N/A` and `TODO` are what a config
template, a README table and a filled-in manifest write after a header
name, and the literal grammar took every one of them, because `/` and
`-` are outside its plain-word class. `abc123def456`,
`sk_live_ex4mple0key0for0tests00` and `12345` carry digits and still
go. The two header names that are `query_params_unambiguous` names as
well - `api-key` and `x-api-key` - are reached by the name-based
rule first, and it applies the same word test to a lone unquoted value,
so `x-api-key: application/json` reads the same way whichever rule sees
it. The name-based rule asks that test wherever the value is a BARE
word, the dotted spelling included, because it strips a leading `.` and
`-` off the name it matched: `gateway.api-key=user-provided` and
`nginx.x-api-key=application/json` keep their word value the way the
bare `api-key: user-provided` always did. It is NOT asked where a quote
opens the value: a quoted literal is a credential whenever its content
holds an ASCII letter or digit, so `authorization: "role-based"` and
`"x-api-key": "not-set"` lose their value while their bare spellings
keep it. That is deliberate - a quote around a value is a writer saying
it is a value - and it is stated as a limit on the docs page rather
than closed. `apikey` without the hyphen
is a parameter name and not a header name under any spelling, so it
takes the exemption under none of them and loses its value under every
spelling: `apikey: not-set` and `svc.apikey=not-set` both go. An
earlier round recorded `svc.apikey=not-set` as untouched; that rested
on a mis-measurement, and the corpus has pinned it redacted throughout,
so nothing in the corpus changes with this correction.
The cost is a limit: a real key of letters alone standing after a
header name is kept. `header_value_terminators` ends the scan at `]`
and `}` as well, so a bracketed log line keeps its closing bracket; no
credential shape holds one. Whatever follows the credential - the
next field of a log line - is kept. With no space after the colon
(`-H authorization:abc123def`) the value is an unquoted literal read by
the literal grammar, so the rest of the command survives and
`-H Authorization:$GH_TOKEN` is left alone. A placeholder value
(`Bearer <YOUR_TOKEN>`) is never redacted.
shapes_comment: `shape_boundary` says where a shape may start: at the start of the
text, after one of the two-character escapes `\n`, `\r` and `\t`,
or after any character that is not a letter or a digit. The escape
stands first in the alternation so it wins in every engine, and
the group is put back in the output, so the break survives. Without
it the character in front of a shape on any line but the first of a
JSON-encoded body is the letter of the escape, which the boundary
refuses: a private key read or written through a tool, and every other
shape, was stored whole there while its raw twin redacted.
In order: the order the shapes are applied in is part of the rule set.
`pattern` is what the two SDKs compile. `linear_engine_pattern`, where it
is present, is what the server compiles instead, for one of two reasons.
On the PEM shape it is the counted bound: the server's engine does not
backtrack, so it does not need the bound that stops a backtracking engine
from restarting a forward scan at every candidate start, and it pays for
that bound in states. On every other deviating shape it is a lookahead:
the server's engine has none, so the SDK pattern's lookaheads are dropped
from the pattern it compiles and listed in `checks`, which the server
applies in code to each match. `right_boundary` refuses a match followed
by [A-Za-z0-9], so a fixed-length shape does not eat the head of a longer
word: ASIAPACIFICREGION2026 is a word, not an AWS key id.
`digit_in_tail` and `not_file_extension` are the OpenAI shape's: its run
accepts the `-` and `_` an ordinary branch name or file name is full of,
so it takes a run only when the run holds a digit and is not followed by
a file extension - a `.` and one to four letters. sk-refactor-
authentication and docs/sk-quickstart-guide-2026.md are names; a
sk-proj- key is a key.
Measured, on 1.8 MB of text that opens PEM blocks it never closes: the
server's engine takes 5.7 ms unbounded and 7.7 s bounded. Measured the
other way, on 210 KB of the same text: CPython 3.11 takes 5.1 s unbounded
and 0.44 s bounded, Bun 1.3 takes 377 ms and 31 ms. The JWT segments carry
no bound anywhere: the segment
class cannot be followed by the `.` that must come next, so the run never
backtracks. The PEM body is tempered: it holds base64 and
the punctuation a PEM header line uses and the two-character escapes
`\n`, `\r` and `\t`, singly or doubly escaped - a key written with
the Write tool reaches the recorder JSON-encoded, so every line break
in its body is a backslash and an `n`, and a key that already lives
inside a JSON file (a service-account `sa.json`) is encoded a second
time, so the same break arrives as two backslashes and an `n` - and a
`-` in it may not open a
second `-----` run, so an unclosed block no longer swallows the prose
after it up to the next block's end. See TOKEN_SHAPES in crates/sasy-redaction/src/lib.rs.
literal_comment: Outside a query string a name is not enough: `password=None`,
`password=os.environ['PW']`, `--password=*)` and `api_key=API_KEY)` are
ordinary source, and a rule that ran to the next space rewrote them and
ate what followed. So every name-based rule outside a query string reads
its value with one grammar. A quoted value - opened by ", ' or a
backtick - is read to the matching unescaped quote on the same line (a
backslash escapes the next character and both stay); the quotes stay and
the content becomes `[redacted]`, and an empty quoted string is left
alone. Two further rules hold of the quoted reading, and of the
double-encoded `\"`-opened reading identically; both are LOCAL to the
value, so nothing earlier on the line is scanned. (1) A quoted value
never crosses a line break: the raw reading stops at a CR or an LF, the
double-encoded reading stops at those and at the two-character `\n`
and `\r` as well, and a quote with no closer before the break opens no
value at all. (2) A quoted value whose content carries no ASCII letter
and no digit is not a credential, so `", "`, `"}, "`, `"], "` and
pure punctuation read as no value. A real secret has a letter or a
digit and stands on one line; a PEM key spans lines, and the PEM shape,
not this reader, is what redacts one. Together they are what keeps
`{"stdout": "Enter password: ", "exit_code": 1}` - what sudo, ssh,
mysql and gpg print into a captured stdout - byte-for-byte, where
reading `", "` as the value wrote the marker over the `, ` between two
members and left a blob no JSON parser accepts. The residual is stated
as a limit: a closing quote followed on the SAME line by more quoted
text that does hold letters (`echo "password: " >> notes.txt && echo
"done"`) is still read as an opener, because without the host grammar
the reader cannot tell a closer from an opener on one line. An earlier
round answered that with a backward scan for an open string; it was
removed. It guarded one of the two quoted branches, it turned an
apostrophe anywhere earlier on the line into a fail-open that stored a
real credential whole, and it made the header-in-text pass quadratic
(19 s on a 200 KB curl trace). A quote of the OTHER character still
opens (`{"cmd": "mysql --password='hunter2'"}`) and an escaped quote
neither opens nor closes.
An unquoted value is a run of `literal_value_chars` ending at one
of `literal_terminators` or at the end of the input; a run stopped by
anything else (a `$`, a `[`, a `{`) is an expansion or a subscript and
is left as written.
The optional backslash in front of the closing quote of the name reads
a name in double-encoded text - an OAuth response body quoted back into
a tool result writes `\"access_token\"` - and the value then reads to
the matching escaped quote, keeping both escapes.
An unquoted value that begins with `=` is not a value at
all: the separator matched the first character of a two-character
operator, so `password == x`, `===`, Make's `:=` and Go's short
assignment are left as written. A credential literal never begins with
an `=` either - base64 padding only ever ends a run.
What is left is redacted only when it is not a
`placeholder_value` and does not start with a `placeholder_prefix`, and
it carries a digit, or a character outside [A-Za-z_.], or is at least 16
characters long. The length clause does not reach a run of word
characters holding a `.` and no digit: that is an attribute path -
`settings.DATABASE_PASSWORD`, `process.env.DB_PASSWORD`,
`self._resolve_password` - and a reference is never redacted whatever
its length. `correcthorsebatterystaple` has no dot and still goes.
The length clause does not reach a bare name either, in one shape: an
`=` with whitespace on BOTH sides of it whose NAME is not an
environment-style upper-case one (`password = `, `api_key = `, `const
password = `), where the value is made only of letters and underscores
and carries an underscore or a change of case.
`DEFAULT_ADMIN_PASSWORD`, `getDatabasePassword` and
`CLIENT_SECRET_ENV_NAME` are a constant, a function and a variable, not
credentials. The spacing is the whole of the discriminator, the same
one the empty-value shape below uses. A glued `=` is a literal whatever
the name's case and whatever the value looks like, because that is what
a flag, a shell line and a .env line are written with: `mysql
--password=MyVerySecretPassword`, `export password=MyVerySecretPassword`
and `DB_PASSWORD=DefaultAdminPassword` all lose their value. So does
every colon form, including a YAML `password: DEFAULT_ADMIN_PASSWORD`.
Its cost is a limit: a letters-only camel-case value in a spaced
lowercase-name assignment is read as a reference and left as written.
A bare value that is a JSON number is replaced by a quoted marker
rather than the bare one when - and only when - the colon in front of
it is a JSON member colon: the name was closed by a quote standing
immediately before the separator. The marker then carries the name's
own closing form, `"[redacted]"` after `"password"`,
`\"[redacted]\"` after a double-encoded `\"password\"`, and
`'[redacted]'` after `'password'`. Bare, a number's marker parses back
as an array holding a bareword and the tool-argument blob a policy
reads stops parsing; quoted anywhere else it is worse, because a YAML
or ini line, a logfmt field and the `-u user:pass` flag all read the
same inside a JSON string as outside one, and a raw quote written
there ends the string early - `{"content": "POSTGRES_PASSWORD:
12345"}` stops parsing and `@json_get_str` hands the policy a
truncated command. So every other colon takes the bare marker.
The `name_value_separator` may consume space on either side of the
`=`, and one spacing says the value is empty rather than standing on
the far side of it: no space before the `=` and space after it, as in
`password= host=db.internal` and `mysql --password= --host=db`. There
nothing is redacted, because the next word is the next field, not the
value. `a = b` is spaced on both sides and `a=b` on neither, and both
read as before; the `:` separator is untouched by this, because
`password: host=db` is a YAML value.
The short all-letters value (`pw`, `secret`) is a
documented limit: taking it would rewrite ordinary source.
env_name_comment: A snake_case name [A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]* ending in one of
`env_name_suffixes`, after a `param_delimiter`, followed by a
`name_value_separator` and a value read by the literal grammar. This is
how a secret arrives most often: a .env file, a `docker run -e` line, a
Makefile, an `export`, a docker-compose `environment:` block, a
GitHub Actions `env:` mapping. The name must END in a suffix, so
`MAX_TOKENS` and `TOKEN_BUDGET` are content.
A Kubernetes pod `env:` list is NOT this shape and is not read. It
writes the name and the value on two lines of their own - `- name:
DB_PASSWORD` and then `value: s3cr3tpg` - so the name and the value
never stand on the same line and no rule here sees them together.
Reading it would mean carrying state from one line to the next,
which no rule in this set does, and the value line's own name,
`value`, is a word nothing may key on. Such a list is stored as
written; a corpus row pins it and the docs name it as a limit.
Every suffix needs at least one character in front of it, so the same
rule reads a name with no prefix at all only through
`env_bare_names`, matched as a whole name: `SECRET_KEY=` (Django and
Flask), `ACCESS_KEY=` and `PRIVATE_KEY=` were read by no rule and
stored whole, while `APP_SECRET_KEY=` and `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=`
lost their values. The list is three names rather than an optional
prefix on every suffix, because the bare form of each of the others is
either an unambiguous name already (`SECRET`, `API_KEY`,
`AUTH_TOKEN`, `PASSWORD`) or the ambiguous `TOKEN`, which is read only
inside a query string. A generic `_KEY` is not a credential suffix:
`CACHE_KEY=users:42`, `SSH_KEY_PATH=~/.ssh/id_ed25519` and
`PUBLIC_KEY=ssh-ed25519 AAAA...` are content, and the last of them is
public by name.
The separator for a PREFIXED name is the full one and not a bare `=`,
so `NAME: value`, `NAME = value` and `NAME=value` all read - the colon
form is how every compose file, k8s manifest, Actions workflow and Helm
values file writes it, and it is the likeliest place of all for a
password to reach a recorded Write or Read.
The three `env_bare_names` read under `name_equals_separator` instead,
which is the same separator with the colon taken out, and they are a
pattern of their own applied in the same pass. A colon after a bare
`private_key`, `secret_key` or `access_key` is a type annotation far
more often than a value - `def sign(private_key:
EllipticCurvePrivateKey, data: bytes) -> bytes:` and `secret_key:
SecretKeyProviderProtocol` are ordinary source, and the length clause
took the type and left the line unreadable. So `SECRET_KEY=...` and
`PRIVATE_KEY = "..."` are read and `private_key: Ed25519PrivateKey`
is not. A YAML `secret_key: <value>` is the cost, and it is a limit.
The delimiter is `param_delimiter` and not a class of its own: that
class excludes the `-`, so a name at the start of a git diff's removed
line had no legal delimiter in front of it and `-DB_PASSWORD=old1234pw`
was stored whole while `+DB_PASSWORD=hunter2new` was scrubbed. A
rotated credential is exactly what stands on the removed line.
The name is compared ASCII-case-insensitively, so the AWS CLI's own
spelling of the file it writes - `aws_secret_access_key = ...` in
~/.aws/credentials - reads as well as `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=`. No
other rule reaches it: the `_` before `secret` is not a delimiter, by
design, so that `OPENAI_API_KEY` is not read as an `api_key` parameter.
The cost of the case-insensitive reading is that an ordinary identifier
ending in a suffix is read too - a `next_token: abc123` pagination
cursor loses its value.
Make's own operators are not covered: `PASSWORD ?= hunter2` and
`PASSWORD += hunter2` are stored as written, and `PASSWORD := hunter2`
is left alone by the rule that refuses a value beginning with `=`.
Only `NAME=value`, `NAME: value` and `NAME = value` are read.
user_password_flag_comment: curl, wget and git all take `-u user:pass`, `--user user:pass` and
`--user=user:pass`. The user part is kept - it says which account the
call was made as - and what follows the first `:` is read by the literal
grammar. The delimiter in front of the flag counts the
two-character escapes as well, for the same reason `param_delimiter`
does: a command on the second line of a JSON-encoded body begins after
space_chars_comment: Every character Unicode calls whitespace, written out character for
character instead of `\s`, and used wherever a URL run, a URL userinfo
field or a `param_value` has to stop at a space. The three regex engines
read `\s` differently - Python narrows it to the five ASCII spaces under
re.ASCII, JavaScript counts U+FEFF as one - so a URL followed by a
no-break space, which is what a browser, a PDF and French typography
emit, is whitespace to one engine's `\s` and not to another's, so the
word after it would be read differently. The class is spelled character
for character, so every engine stops in the same places. U+FEFF is not
in it: it is not Unicode whitespace. JavaScript reads it as a space
elsewhere, which is the difference the known limits name.
url_comment: `url_in_text` ends the run at the backslash as well as at a quote, so a
JSON-escaped URL leaves the blob parseable and the rest of the command
intact. Before redacting, trailing `url_trailing_punctuation` is trimmed
off the run and put back afterwards, so a markdown link keeps its closing
paren; idempotence does not depend on the trim, because a field whose
value already begins `[redacted` is left alone. `url_userinfo` takes the
password out of a `scheme://user:password@host` authority in any scheme -
a git remote in a `fatal: unable to access` line, a `postgresql://`
connection string - keeping the scheme, the user and the host. The user
part may be empty: `redis://:password@host` is how the Redis and AMQP
clients document a password with no account name, and it is still a
run is bounded and needs a left boundary so a megabyte of letters is not
rescanned from every position. That boundary is the one place that needs
no two-character escape of its own: after `\n` the character in front
of the scheme is the letter of the escape, and a letter is what a scheme
begins with, so the letter joins the scheme run and the authority is read
either way. Two corpus rows pin it, one after `\n` and one after `\t`.
